== Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:470-635

\section{Coercion Resolution}
\seclabel{resolving-coercion}
For a given functional call, we first determine whether there exists a
declaration that is applicable without coercion.  If so, the most
specific declaration is selected; if not, then coercions are
explicitly added to the functional call.  If more than one coercion is
possible then the coercion that yields the most specific type is
chosen.  \secref{restrictions-coercion} and
\chapref{overloaded-declarations} describe overloading rules for the
declarations of coercions and overloaded functionals that guarantee
there exists always a most specific coercion when two or more are possible.

We first define a notion of more specific types in the presence of coercion.
Recall from \secref{type-relations} that Fortress defines an
\emph{exclusion} relation between types which is denoted by $\excludes$.

For types $T$ and $U$, we say that $T$ \emph{rejects} $U$,
and write $T \rejects U$, if for all coercions to $T$, the type coerced
from excludes $U$:
\[
T \rejects U \iff \forall A: A \coercedefto T \implies A \excludes U.
\]
Note that $T \rejects U$ implies $U \not\coercesto T$.

We say that $T$ is \emph{no less specific} than $U$, and write $T
\morespecificeq U$, if $T$ is a subtype of $U$ or $T$ excludes, can be
coerced to, and rejects $U$:
\[
T \morespecificeq U \iff
T \Ovrsubtype U \logicor
(T \excludes U \logicand T \coercesto U \logicand T \rejects U).
\]

The $\morespecificeq$ relation is reflexive and antisymmetric but not
necessarily transitive.  It is possible, for example, for
three types, $T$, $U$ and $V$, each excluding the other two,
to have coercions from $T$ to $U$ and from $U$ to $V$.  In
this case, $T \morespecificeq U$ and $U \morespecificeq V$ but
$T \not\morespecificeq V$.

Notice that if two tuple types have a bijective correspondence
between their element types then the $\morespecificeq$ relationship between
the tuple types is equivalent to applying the $\morespecificeq$
relation elementwise.

We say that $T$ is \emph{more specific} than $U$, and write $T
\morespecific U$, if $T \morespecificeq U \logicand T \neq U$.

We extend the definitions of no less specific and more specific to
declarations.  We say that a declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{no less
specific} than a declaration $\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \morespecificeq \Qs$.
Similarly, we say that a declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{no less
specific} than a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ if $(\Ps_0, \Ps)
\morespecificeq (\Qs_0, \Qs)$.  A declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more
specific} than a declaration $\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$.
Similarly, a declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more specific} than
a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ if $(\Ps_0, \Ps) \morespecific (\Qs_0,
\Qs)$.

Now we describe how to determine which coercion is applied to a given
call in terms of rewriting functional calls.  The rewriting is
for pedagogical purposes; implementation techniques may vary.

Consider a static call $\f(\As)$ or $\As_0.\f(\As)$.  Let $\Sigma$ be
the set of parameter types of functional declarations of $\f$ that are
applicable to the call.
Let $\Sigma'$ be the set of parameter types of
functional declarations of $\f$ that are
applicable with coercion to the call.
If $\Sigma$ is not empty then we use the overloading resolution
described in \secref{resolving-overloading} to determine which
element of $\Sigma$ is called.
If $\Sigma$ is empty but $\Sigma'$ is not, then we rewrite the call as
follows.  Define: \[\mathpzc{C} = \{T \in \Sigma' \mid S \coercedefto T
\logicand \As \Ovrsubtype S\}.\] Let $T \in \mathpzc{C}$ be the most
specific element of $\mathpzc{C}$.  In other words, there does not exist
$T' \in \mathpzc{C}$ such that $T' \morespecific T$.  The restrictions
given in \secref{restrictions-coercion} and
\chapref{overloaded-declarations} guarantee that such a $T$
exists and that it is unique.  The call $\f(\As)$ or $\As_0.\f(\As)$ is
rewritten to \EXP{f(\mathrm{coercion}\llbracket{T}\rrbracket(\TYP{A}))} or
\EXP{A_{0}.f(\mathrm{coerce}\llbracket{T}\rrbracket(A))}
and the declaration with parameter
type $T$ is applied to the call.

As an example, consider the following definitions:
%trait ZZ32 excludes { ZZ64, ZZ128 } end
%trait ZZ64 excludes { ZZ128 }
%  coerce(z:ZZ32) = ...
%end
%trait ZZ128
%  coerce(z:ZZ32) = ...
%  coerce(z:ZZ64) = ...
%end
%
%f(z:ZZ64) = 1
%f(z:ZZ128) = 2
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}32 \KWD{excludes} \{\,\mathbb{Z}64, \mathbb{Z}128\,\} \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}64 \KWD{excludes} \{\,\mathbb{Z}128\,\}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}32) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}128\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}32) = \ldots\)\\
\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
\(f(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64) = 1\)\\
\(f(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}128) = 2\)
\end{Fortress}
Then the call \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}32)} resolves to the
declaration \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}64)} because $\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
\morespecific \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}$, which follows from the facts that
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} excludes \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}, coerces to it, and rejects it:
the one type that coerces to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, excludes
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}.
The same facts make the two declarations of \VAR{f} a valid overloading, and the
exclusion of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} by \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} does the same for the two
coercions to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128} (\secref{more-specific-rule}).
\revision{revival-coercion-example}{The Working Draft of February 2011 declared the
three traits with no \KWD{excludes} clause and said that the resolution follows
from the fact that \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} coerces to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}.
By the definition above, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} is then not more specific than
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}, and neither the two declarations of \VAR{f} nor the two
coercions to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128} are a valid overloading; both implementations
of the revival refuse the example as the Working Draft wrote it.
The clauses added are spelled as \library\ spell those of their integer types,
each trait excluding the wider ones.}

Notice that coercion is resolved statically.  Once a coercion is
statically chosen for a call, this coercion is conceptually inserted
into the call.
This means that the statically chosen coercion is applied at run time.

For example, in the following program:
%trait A
%  coerce(c:C) = ...
%end
%trait B excludes A end
%trait C end
%object D extends {B,C} end
%
%f(a:A) = 3
%f(b:B) = 4
%
%c : C = D
%f(c)
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} A\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(c\COLONOP{}C) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} B \KWD{excludes} A \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} C \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{object} D \KWD{extends} \{B,C\} \KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
\(f(a\COLONOP{}A) = 3\)\\
\(f(b\COLONOP{}B) = 4\)\\[4pt]
\(c \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} C = D\)\\
\(f(c)\)
\end{Fortress}
the call to \EXP{f(C)} resolves to the declaration
%\EXP{f(a\COLONOP{}A)}
\EXP{f(A)} despite the fact that the declaration
%\EXP{f(b\COLONOP{}B)}
\EXP{f(B)} is
%dynamically directly
applicable to the dynamic call \EXP{f(D)} and does not require
coercion.

== Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:254-273

\subsection{GCD, LCM, and CHOOSE Operators}

The infix operator \OPR{GCD} computes the greatest common
divisor of its integer operands, and \OPR{LCM} computes the least
common multiple.  The operator \OPR{CHOOSE} computes binomial
coefficients:
\EXP{n \OPR{CHOOSE} k = \binom{n}{k} = { n! \over k!(n-k)! }}.

The results of \OPR{GCD} and \OPR{LCM} are nonnegative
(\secref{basic-integers}).
On a fixed-size integer type, by the rule for integer results above, a result that the type
cannot hold throws an \TYP{IntegerOverflow}: on \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, for example,
the greatest common divisor of \EXP{-2^{31}} and \EXP{0} is \EXP{2^{31}}, and
the least common multiple of \EXP{2^{31}-1} and \EXP{2} is \EXP{2^{32}-2},
neither of which \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} holds.
\revision{revival-gcd}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said neither that these
results are nonnegative nor what happens when one does not fit its type.}

The expression \EXP{e \neq e'} is semantically equivalent to the expression
\EXP{\neg(e = e')}.

The second gate still re-ran the count and distance stages, 800 s for the distance, and both tables came out the same as the first gate's but for their seconds and machine lines (`RECORD.md:304`). This is new: the script runs the full gate after any repair (`climb-batch-workflow.js:1894-1907`).
- **The cache-off runs.** Two whole-stage runs, stopped after 30 minutes each (finding 4).

### What the reviews cost, in these tokens

- From `summary.txt` section 8, each review agent's context at its last turn: the conformance review of 6b and 7, 539K; of 7R, 461K; the process review of the three, 454K.
- Against the runs: 7R's review is 15% of 7R's 3.15M. This single review ended at about 0.5M, 14% of 7C's 3.71M. The earlier note's 4% was in ITE, which weights re-reads by the cache price; in the harness's count a review is about a seventh of a batch.
- Yield here: findings 1, 2 and 4 are placements that would have reached batch 7b's and N's planners wrong. Finding 3 and 72 are notes.

### Measures the evidence supports, each with its cost

1. **Put the ruling into the rule** (the earlier note's measure 3, now a third repeat). One sentence in `climb-batch-workflow.md`'s rule text, which the prefix repeats: a settled defect gets its gated test in the batch that measures it; "the prelude leaves", "a later rung writes it" and "the rung's files exclude a test" do not defer it; the repair round writes it (6b's, 7R's and 7C's judges). Cost: one sentence, before the next launch.
2. **Reuse the first gate's count and distance tables after a repair** that touches no library, checker or interpreter source, as the decision of 14:18 does for a rung's before. Saves about 15 minutes of machine time per repaired batch. It is a change to the script's gate step.
3. **Probe a shadow adversarially before its code is put to you.** A judgement that puts code up for approval has the skeptic's probes run on the shadow first, or names the shapes it did not try. Here two defects of the approved lines were found in the first hours after launch. Cost: one skeptic pass per shadow, about 0.4M tokens.
4. **A parked line says only what was sent.** Where a rung's "What comes back to Pavol" list is filed, the line says whether the landing message carried it or it is on file only.

Each item the batch opened, left or listed, with its home on `main` at `88ccf8217`. The routing commit filed most of them; this checks each.

**Rows the batch opened.**
- 487 (another unit's type below a generic subtrait, not caught): batch 8's line (`PLAN.md:76`). Has a home. Its repair is a new checker rule at object declarations, derived from the value reading and not copied from Welterweight's D-Object (row 487's note); batch 8's planner should read it as a checker rung.

`explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:464`: "The prelude's `#` has no compiled gate of its own").

- **It proves too much.** "The prelude leaves at the switch-over" applies word for word to the split,

content.content:
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point), then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$
be the radix) has the following type:
\begin{Fortress}
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
\end{Fortress}
where $v$ is the value of the $n$-digit numeral, with the radix point
deleted, interpreted in radix $r$.

Every numeral also has type
\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n}, \VAR{m}, \VAR{r}, and \VAR{v}.


Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types
because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect them to be polymorphic.
For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
converting it immediately to a floating-point number
may lose precision.
If that numeral is used in an expression
involving floating-point intervals,
it would be better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).


\marginnote{What is an ``integer'' in this context?}
In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
this is true regardless of whether
the integers are of type $\mathbb{Z}$ (or \txt{ZZ}),
$\mathbb{Z}64$ (or \txt{ZZ64}), $\mathbb{N}32$ (or \txt{NN32}), or
whatever.  Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of rationals
are always exact; thus values such as \EXP{1/3} are represented exactly in
Fortress.

\note{We should give an example with a radix specifier.}
Numerals containing a radix point are actually rational
literals; thus \EXP{3.125} has the rational value \EXP{3125/1000}.
The quotient of two integer literals is a static expression
(described in \secref{static-expr}) whose value is rational.
Similarly, a sequence of digits with a radix point followed by the symbol
$\times$ and an integer literal raised to an integer literal,
such as \EXP{6.0221415 \times 10^{23}}
is a static expression whose value is rational.
If such static expressions are mentioned as part of a floating-point
computation, the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then
converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring
at most one floating-point rounding error.
But in general rational computations may also be performed at run time,
not just at compile time.

## 12. Decisions, each with the ways not taken

- **The lock's shape.** Candidates:
  - `synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name))` around the whole of `loadClass`, which is the loader's own monitor. Taken.
  - The same with `registerAsParallelCapable`, one lock per name.
  - A lock only in `loadClosureClass`.
  - A `ConcurrentHashMap` of futures per name.

  The monitor is the lock the JVM already holds when it resolves a class through a loader that is not parallel-capable, and it is what the JDK's own `loadClass` takes. Explicit loads (`loadClosureClass`, `getRTTIclass`, the union instantiation) were the only ones running without it. Taking it adds no lock order the implicit loads do not already have: a generation step that initialises another class under the monitor, as `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java:274` can, already does so on every implicit load. Per-name locks would admit two loads each holding one name's lock while generating a class that needs the other's; the JDK leaves them off unless a loader opts in. A lock in `loadClosureClass` alone leaves the other two explicit callers racing. Futures would change the loader's structure for no gain the measurement can see.
- **Where `history` is written.** Left before `defineClass`. Under the lock no other thread can see the name before its class is defined. Moving the write would change what the same thread does if generation re-enters the loader for the name it is generating, which it does not today by reading, and every single-thread run would need re-measuring for no gain. The pre-existing behaviour after a failed load, where the name stays in `history` and a later load of it returns null (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:189-193`), is unchanged; by reading, not measured.
- **Binding a catch name always.** The grammar makes the name mandatory (`try.tex:22`), and the specification binds it (`:56-60`), so every catch clause's code changes: `getValue`, a cast and a store in place of a pop. The prelude has no `catch`, so no library class moves. The other way, binding only a name the body reads, needs a free-variable test at each clause and saves three instructions.
- **Binding a typecase clause's name only when it has one.** Clauses without a name pop as before, which is why only `cast`'s template changed in the prelude.
- **The identity functions' values of type `T`.** Two ways were on file:
  - A typed binding, `v: ZZ32 = 0` then `cast[\T\](v)`, which converts a numeral by coercion on the compiled path and keeps walk's value as it is (FACTS.md, "Under walk, the interpreter converts by coercion at its three kinds of type check", FACTS.md:110). Taken, in the two branches that passed a numeral.
  - A checker refinement that binds `T` inside a witness branch (`explorations/reviews/sum-replacement-judgement.md` section 7, check 3), which is Scala and not this rung's. Not taken.

  `typed` would not do: the compiled path has no `forAsExpr`. The six branches that pass a function's result (`widen`, `unsigned`, `big`, `Ratio`, `narrow`) already have values of their type on both paths and are unchanged.
- **Row 420's fix is row 419's.** No separate edit was made; the row closes with 419, its cause located and gated.
- **Home 3, not home 2, for a dispatcher that is not a template.** The batch record plans home 2 for both remainders "where the rung shows it failing" (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-6.5.md:188`). For generic dotted methods the rung took it (`XXXDispatchMethodArmRungG`). For a dispatcher that is not a template the alternative was an `XXX` test asserting only that the call does not throw and answers one of the two declarations. It was not taken, because the chapter as committed forbids the pair (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:102-105`), so no passage says which answer a test should hold, and the grep of section 9 finds none; home 3, the probes and row 496.
- **Two more compiled tests than the brief named.** `WitnessIdentityRungG` is answer 7's identity shape in the compiler's world. It is the judgement's check 3, `zeroOf[\RR64\]()` through a repaired `cast`, now gated. `XXXDispatchMethodArmRungG` is the remainder's home 2.

## 13. What waits

- **A compiled `SUM`'s identity end to end** waits for the switch-over. The compiler's own library has no generic `SUM` (FACTS.md, "The compile ladder loses one file to an approved test line, until the switch-over", FACTS.md:92). `WitnessIdentityRungG` gates the device, and the one library's two functions are checked under walk only.

- **The dispatch remainder**, sections 9 and 10.

## 9. The dispatch change's reach and its remainder

The change reads every declared generic arm with as many static parameters as the template dispatcher at the dispatcher's parameters by position, when the dispatcher's own static parameters are all of type kind; the arm's kinds are not checked (`OverloadSet.java:1342-1353`, the kind test at `:1350`), the parameters the loader has set to the call site's. It covers top-level generic functions whose dispatcher is a template, which the three programs are. Measured before and after, compiled at both thread counts (`differential-before.txt`, `differential-after.txt`):
- **An arm in the more-specific relation that is not the dispatcher's by position** is now tested at the call's instantiation, where it was tested at an instantiation read from the value. For `f[\T\](x: T)` beside `f[\U\](x: Box[\U\])` reached through a generic caller (`SkPosBox`), and for `grab[\Y\](t: Fixed[\Y\])` with `Fixed[\Y\] extends Tag[\Blue\]` (`SkPosFixed`), the compiled answer moved from the more specific arm to the less specific one, `box` to `any` and `fixed` to `tag`, at both thread counts (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/probes/skeptic/dispatch-pos.txt:6`, `:17`, `:38`, `:45`). `Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-107` with `:136-138` gives the new answer, and `:173-175` and `:292-295` the old one. Today's checker accepts both pairs; answer 9's narrow rule refuses both once built (POSITIONS 2026-09-26, answer 9). No gated verdict moves (`compare-generic-overload.txt`). Row 499, home 3 until then.
- **Generic dotted methods** keep both defects. `MethRenamed`, `MethSwapped` and `MethZZ32` (the three programs as methods of one object) die with the same `ClassCastException` before and after. The specification settles them as it settles the top-level ones (section 4), so they get home 2: `compiler_tests/XXXDispatchMethodArmRungG.fss` with `XXXDispatchMethodArmRungG.test` (run) and `DispatchMethodArmRungGLink.test` (link), failing as expected (`junit-after.txt:118`). Walk cannot run them, because it infers no static argument for a method call (row 21).
- **A dispatcher that is not a template**, a generic declaration beside a plain one, keeps both defects. `PlainBesideZZ32` dies on the `ZZ32` spelling and `PlainBesideRet` on the unrewritten `Marker⟦X⟧` (before and after). Answer 9 makes the pair legal, but the specification as committed still forbids it (`overloading.tex:103-105`), and which declaration applies when the call site resolved to the plain one is not written anywhere. The grep behind that, `grep -n 'static parameters' Specification/basic/overloading.tex Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, gives `overloading.tex:102-107` (the sentence), `:167`, `:173-175` and `:205` (inference before applicability), `:292-295` (inference before specificity) and `Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:95-103` ("identical (up to α-equivalence)"); none of them says which declaration applies at run time to a call resolved to a declaration without static parameters. Walk answers both ways: "the Any declaration" for `PlainBesideZZ32` (`differential-after.txt:346`) and `Marker[Red]` for `PlainBesideRet` (`:362`). are not a valid overloading; they are unambiguous declarations.
An operator method declaration whose name is one of the operator parameters
(described in \secref{opr-ident})
of its enclosing trait or object may be overloaded with other operator
declarations in the same component.
Therefore, such an operator method declaration
must satisfy the overloading rules
(described in \chapref{overloaded-declarations})
with every operator declaration in the same component.

\note{This restriction will be relaxed.}

Although there may be multiple declarations
with the same functional name,
it is an error for their static parameters to differ
(up to $\alpha$-equivalence),
or for one declaration to have static parameters
and another to not have them.
Hence, static parameters do not enter into the determination of which
declarations are applicable,
so we ignore them for most of this chapter.



Recall from \chapref{types} that we write
$T \Ovrsubtype U$ when $T$ is a subtype of $U$,
and $T \strictsubtype U$ when $T \Ovrsubtype U$ and $T \neq U$.


\section{Applicability to Named Functional Calls}
\seclabel{functional-applicability}
In this section, we show how to determine which declarations are
applicable to a named functional call when all declarations have only
ordinary parameters (i.e., neither varargs nor keyword parameters).

For the purpose of defining applicability, a named functional call can
be characterized by the name of the functional and its argument type.
Recall that a functional has a single parameter, which may be a tuple
(a dotted method has a receiver as well).
 We abuse notation by using
\emph{static call $\f(\As)$} to refer to a named functional call with
name $\f$ and whose argument has static type $\As$, and
\emph{dynamic call $\f(\Xs)$} to refer to a named functional call with
We use \emph{call $\f(\Cs)$} to refer to a named functional call with
name $\f$ and whose argument, when evaluated, has dynamic type $\Cs$.
(Note that if the type system is sound---and we certainly hope that
it is!---then $\Xs \Ovrsubtype \As$ for all well-typed calls to $\f$.)
We use the term \emph{call $\f(\Cs)$} to refer to static and dynamic calls
collectively.
We assume throughout this chapter that all static variables in functional calls
have been instantiated or inferred.

9:In plain words: when a program calls a generic function without writing its type arguments, the checker works them out from the arguments. Today it uses only subtyping, so `scale(b, 3)` for a box of `RR64` is refused although `3` converts to `RR64`, and a `ZZ32` beside a `ZZ64` gives a union type instead of `ZZ64`. Walk makes the same mistakes at run time. And a numeral such as `3` is typed three ways today: the compiled checker calls it `IntLiteral`, the one library declares that `IntLiteral` below `ZZ32`, and walk makes it a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by its size. This batch makes both paths infer with coercion, then gives the numeral its own type.
15:- **Q, the numeral's own type.** The one library takes the compiler library's sibling `IntLiteral` with a coercion into each number type, walk gives every integer numeral that type, and the library's numeral sites are respelled where the switch needs it. Library and Java.
23:- Today both paths answer `ZZ32`: walk gives a numeral the narrowest of `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and `ZZ` that holds it, and the checker's `IntLiteral` is declared below `ZZ32`. Once a numeral has its own type that converts into every number type (your decision on a numeral's type), nothing picks one: `ZZ32` and `NN32` both take a numeral and neither converts into the other. The specification never wrote a default; its numeral hierarchy is a note ("We need to describe the Numeral type hierarchy").
24:- The specification's coercion resolution has no answer for the second case: it says a unique most specific coercion always exists by its restrictions on coercion declarations (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:470-480`, `:626-660`), which forbid only a coercion from a subtype and a cycle; a type that coerces into two mutually excluding types, which a sibling `IntLiteral` is, escapes them, and neither `ZZ32` nor `NN32` is more specific by its definition (`:493-506`), so a rule is needed whichever option is taken; walk's rung C already says "Ambiguous coercion" there.
32:- **Recommended: 1.** It is what both paths do today, the one library's own practice (its `IntLiteral` below `ZZ32`, the team's placeholder "until coercion is implemented") and the compiler library's (its first numeral coercion was into `ZZ32`, `128f313b5`, 2009; its ranges over `ZZ32`); and it follows three decisions of yours: the JVM principle (2026-09-22, Java's default where it makes sense, corrected where precision or performance asks; an unfixed numeral as an unbounded `ZZ` would put a bignum in every such loop), a size's range (2026-09-27, an `int` parameter is a `ZZ32`) and ranges over `ZZ32` ("the largest array size on JVM"). It is taken overnight at (1) unless you answer, since it reverses no decision of yours, and listed for your review (POSITIONS 2026-09-27, the numerics plans, the standing reading).
38:- **Row 437 closes on walk only; row 432 by reading.** A type parameter has no coercions (the specification's rule), so the checker still refuses `matrix(v)`'s numeral `0` for `NN32` elements; walk's half closes with Q. `SUM <|1, 2, 3|>` closes only if Q's `IntLiteral` carries the algebra its arithmetic implies, as every flat number type does; not measured.
39:- **Walk converts a body to its declared return type** (row 387), in Q: under the switch `getter zero(): ZZ32 = 0` would otherwise return an `IntLiteral` (plan-6.5 probe, by reading).
58:- Run 2: every integer numeral under walk is an `IntLiteral`; the one library's `IntLiteral` is a number type of its own with a coercion into `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` and its own arithmetic; walk converts a body to its declared return type; the library's numeral sites that the switch breaks are respelled; the literals section and the coercion chapter's note are revised in the S1 form.
67:- **The numerics plans**, 2026-09-27, the synthesis's decision 3: "Agreed." (19:30 UTC), option 1. "The inference rule lands with the numeral switch as one batch, batch N, after the ranges batch and before 7b: the checker infers a static argument with coercion (answer 8's promotion rule, the narrowest type every number argument converts into, is its number case) and keeps the expected type at a call written `f(x)` with a retry without it, so that a binding's coercion still applies; walk does the same at dispatch; the one library and walk take the compiler library's sibling `IntLiteral` with its coercions (the numeral switch of 2026-09-27, which cannot land alone: measured, it refuses 13 C4 and 11 APL declarations, and row 401's shape in `heads`, `unheads` and `onehot`); the specification's type-inference chapter is written in the S1 form and lands only with the checker rung. Four rungs: checker, walk, library, specification. It closes batch 6.5's question 1. A worker measures the rule on a checker shadow before the batch is briefed." The shadow is `explorations/reviews/inference-rule-shadow.md`. The same entry's decision 5 is the order (7, 7R, N, 7b, 8, with 6.5 in the slots a decision leaves), and its last sentences are the standing go for phase 3's batches, the pre-approved Fable review of each record, and the reading that a question a record raises overnight takes its recommended default unless that default reverses a decision of his.
68:- **A numeral's type**, 2026-09-27: "walk needs to be corrected and switched to using IntLiteral"; "yes, go ahead" to the one library taking the compiler library's `IntLiteral`, "a numeral's own type that each number type converts from", the implementers' later word weighing more than the unfinished text; "with the changed interpreter outputs measured first; a real choice the measurement finds comes to him in the protocol's form. Rows 79, 432, 437 and 443 are its measure."
74:- **The library's practice is the standard**, 2026-09-19; **the library route**, 2026-09-21: nothing is added to the compiler library, whose `IntLiteral` is the model the one library takes.
89:**Its briefing.** The decisions the rung rests on (the numerics plans, answer 8, a numeral's type, route A, the library's practice, the library route, answer 12, the JVM principle, under which Q1's default is read, the probe rule, the launch of phase 3's batches, the stops, rung D's stop); ledger rows 401, 388, 455, 447, 425, 432 and 79; the shadow note's answers and its sections on the edit, the probes, microGPT, the distance, the compiler's tests and the forks, with rule.patch and RuleCRun.fss; the synthesis's decision 3; the Fable plan's faces A and C; evidence B's sections on how a static argument is inferred, whether the expected type is used and whether coercion is considered; measurement D's sections on the other drops and on what the kept context changes; the specification's inference chapter, its sections on applicability with coercion, coercion resolution and applicability to named calls; the checker's applicability methods, checkApplication, the tight juxtaposition's cases, inferStaticParams, the coercion oracle's getCoercionsTo and substitutableFor; the two libraries' IntLiteral; the two expected failures it promotes; the FACTS entries on inference, the expected type, a numeral's type, the coercion refused by an inferred generic, microGPT's checker errors, the specification's silence, the distance, rung R's refusal, the size checks and the harness; the walkthrough's section on how the checker walks the tree and the map's checker row. The keys are in section 7; checks is the decisions (the numerics plans, answer 8, a numeral's type, the JVM principle, the stops), the rows, the shadow's sections on the tests and the forks, rule.patch, the applicability section, the applicability methods, the two tests and the harness entry on a pinned expected failure.
92:- The checker infers a generic's static arguments from the arguments' types by subtyping alone. Its constraint is "argType <: domain", with "range <: context" when a context is given (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:928-947`); the solver binds each variable to the join of its lower bounds, a union (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/Formula.scala:527`); `checkApplicableWithInference` is documented "with static argument inference and no coercion" (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:171-173`), and coercions are built only for a candidate with no static parameter left (`:278-340`). So a numeral or a narrower number for a declared parameter of a generic is refused (row 401: `scale(Box[\3\](2), 3)` with `m: ZZ32`, under the compiler library, whose `IntLiteral` is not a `ZZ32`; row 388: `gf[\T\](x: Wide, y: T)` with a `Narrow`, and the container shape `scale(b, z)` for `b: Box[\RR64\]`), and a call over mixed widths infers a union (`pick(l, 3)` is `OR(ZZ64,IntLiteral)`), where answer 8 names the narrowest type both convert into (FACTS.md, "Static arguments are inferred from the arguments alone, on both paths, and never through a coercion").
96:**The decisions.** The numerics plans, decision 3 (`explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, 2026-09-27): the checker infers a static argument with coercion, answer 8's promotion rule its number case, and keeps the expected type at `f(x)` with a retry without it, so that a binding's coercion still applies. Answer 8 (2026-09-26): a call over mixed widths infers the narrowest type both sides convert into, `ZZ64` for `ZZ32` with `NN32` though neither argument is a `ZZ64`; `ZZ64` does not convert into `RR64`. Under Q1 = (1): a type parameter that only numerals fix, whose bound `IntLiteral` does not meet, takes `ZZ32` (or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` for a numeral whose value `ZZ32` cannot hold, where the value is at hand), and a call whose declarations each take a numeral only by coercion, none most specific, takes the `ZZ32` declaration. Answer 12 (2026-09-26): a size the call cannot fix stays refused at the call (batch 6's rung R, in `checkApplication`). content.content:
\seclabel{basic-integers}

The trait \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} (\STR{ZZ}) encompasses all finite integers,
the results of starting from \EXP{0} and repeatedly adding or subtracting \EXP{1} a finite number of times.

\Library\ also declare four integer types of fixed size.
The five integer types are these:

\begin{tabbing}
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} (\STR{ZZ}) is the set of integers (it coerces from \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}).
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} (\STR{ZZ64}) is the set of integers representable in 64-bit two's-complement form (it coerces from \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}).
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\STR{ZZ32}) is the set of integers representable in 32-bit two's-complement form.
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{N}64} (\STR{NN64}) is the set of integers representable in 64-bit unsigned binary form (it coerces from \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}).
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} (\STR{NN32}) is the set of integers representable in 32-bit unsigned binary form.
\end{tabbing}

Like every number type, each of them is a subtype of \TYP{Number} and of no other
number type (\secref{basic-rationals}), and each coerces into \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}.
An integer type coerces from each other integer type all of whose values it holds,
as listed above; every other conversion between integer types is written explicitly.

Among the explicit conversions, the method \VAR{narrow} converts a value of
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and a value of
\EXP{\mathbb{N}64} to \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, by keeping its low 32 bits: the result
is the value of the narrower type that is congruent to the argument modulo
\EXP{2^{32}}.
A value that the narrower type holds is unchanged; any other wraps, and no
\TYP{IntegerOverflow} is thrown.

The operators \OPR{LSHIFT} and \OPR{RSHIFT} shift the bits of an integer of any of
the five types by a count of any integer type, and return a value of the type of
the integer shifted.
On \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\VAR{shift}(x,k)} and
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\VAR{shift}(x,-k)}.
On a fixed-size type of width \VAR{n}, for a nonnegative count \VAR{k},
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\lfloor x/2^{k} \rfloor}, and
\EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k} is the value of the type that is congruent to
\EXP{x \cdot 2^{k}} modulo \EXP{2^{n}}: the bits shifted out are lost, and no
\TYP{IntegerOverflow} is thrown.
So a count at or beyond the width gives \EXP{0} for a left shift, and for a right
shift \EXP{0}, or \EXP{-1} if \VAR{x} is negative.
A negative count shifts the other way: \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} (-k)} is
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k}, and \EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} (-k)} is \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k}.
The count is read by its value, whatever its type: an \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} count of
\EXP{2^{63}} or more is beyond the width, not negative.
\revision{revival-shifts}{The Working Draft of February 2011 named neither
\VAR{narrow} nor \OPR{LSHIFT} and \OPR{RSHIFT}, which \library\ declare on the
integer types; the two paragraphs above state the rules the revival decided for
them.}

It is often desirable to know that an integer lies in a subset of its type,
such as the positive values or the nonzero values.
As for the rationals, such subsets are not types of their own:

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%

\subsection{Parallel Do Expressions}
\seclabel{also-block}

\note{Reduction variables are not yet supported.}

A series of blocks may be run in parallel using the \KWD{also}
construct.  Any number of contiguous blocks may be joined together by
\KWD{also}.  Each block is run in a separate
implicit thread; these threads together form a group.  The expression
as a whole completes when the group is complete.
A thread can be placed in a particular region by using an \KWD{at} expression
as described in \secref{parallelism-fundamentals}.
When multiple
expression blocks are separated by \KWD{also}, each expression block must
have type \EXP{()}; the result and type of the parallel \KWD{do}
expression is also \EXP{()}.


For example:
-----


The expressions in the \KWD{try} block are first evaluated in order
until they have all completed normally, or until one of them completes
abruptly.  If the \KWD{try} block completes normally, the
\emph{provisional} value of the \KWD{try} expression is the value of the
last expression in the \KWD{try} block.  In this case, and in case of
exiting to an enclosing \KWD{label} expression, the \KWD{catch} and
\KWD{forbid} clauses are ignored.


If an expression in the \KWD{try} block completes abruptly by throwing
an exception, the exception value is bound to the identifier specified in
the \KWD{catch} clause, and the type of the exception is matched
against the subclauses of the \KWD{catch} clause in turn, exactly as in a
\KWD{typecase} expression (\secref{typecase}).
The right-hand-side expression block
of the first matching subclause is evaluated.  If it
completes normally, its value is the provisional value of the
\KWD{try} expression.  If the \KWD{catch} clause completes abruptly,
the \KWD{try} expression completes abruptly.  If a thrown exception is
not matched by the \KWD{catch} clause (or this clause is omitted), but
----
followed by \KWD{of}, a sequence of typecase clauses
(each consisting of a sequence of \emph{guarding types}
followed by the token \EXP{\Rightarrow}, followed by an expression block),
an optional \KWD{else} clause
(consisting of \KWD{else} followed by the token \EXP{\Rightarrow},
followed by an expression block),
and finally \KWD{end}.

A \KWD{typecase} expression with a binding expression
evaluates the expression first;
if it completes normally, the value of the expression is bound
to the identifiers and the first matching typecase clause is chosen.
If there are multiple identifiers, the binding expression must be evaluated
to a tuple value of the same number of elements.
A typecase clause matches if the type of the value bound to each identifier
is a subtype of the corresponding type in the clause.
The expression block of the first matched clause
(and only that clause) is evaluated (see \secref{block-expr}) to yield
the value of the \KWD{typecase} expression.
If no matched clause is found, a \TYP{MatchFailure} exception is thrown
(\TYP{MatchFailure} is an unchecked exception).
Unlike bindings in other contexts,
the static type of such an identifier
is \emph{not} determined by the static type of
the expression it is bound to.
If the static type of a subexpression
in the bindings for a \KWD{typecase} expression has type \VAR{T},
when typechecking each typecase clause,
the static type of the corresponding identifier is the intersection of \VAR{T}
and the corresponding guarding type for that clause.
The type of a \KWD{typecase} expression is the union
of types of all right-hand sides of the typecase clauses.
